balanced.name: Step by step
balanced.description: Build intuition, then develop a complete understanding.
balanced.example:
You look up the same phone number every day. What could make that easier? Keep it on a note nearby, so you do not need to search the directory again.

A cache works similarly: it temporarily stores data somewhere quicker to access. Check the cache first; if the data is missing, return to the original source.

It saves time, but when the source changes, the cached copy may need updating.

socratic.name: Guided questions
socratic.description: Reason through focused questions and hints before the explanation.
socratic.example:
If a weather app contacts a distant server every time you open it, what problems might you notice?

Hint: consider the waiting time and the cost of repeating the same request.

One solution is to keep a recent result nearby and use it again. That is caching. Now consider: if the weather changes, can you keep using that stored result indefinitely?

analogy.name: Everyday analogies
analogy.description: Make abstract ideas concrete through familiar situations.
analogy.example:
Think of data storage as a library, and a cache as your desk.

Keep the books you are using on the desk within reach. Visit the library only when a book is missing. Desk space is limited, so you keep the most useful books nearby.

The analogy has a limit: cached data can be a copy. The library may update its version while the copy on your desk stays unchanged.

practical.name: Learning by doing
practical.description: Try a small task, then learn the principle from the result.
practical.example:
Try this: open a document you use often, find a fact you repeatedly look up, and copy it onto a sticky note.

Next time, check the note first. If the information is missing, look in the document and add it to the note.

You have just simulated a cache. Now change the original document and check the note. What rule would keep your copy up to date?

concise.name: Straight to the point
concise.description: Key idea first, one example, minimal preamble.
concise.example:
A cache temporarily stores data you may need again, avoiding repeated retrieval.

Example: keep a frequently used phone number on a note nearby.

Read order: check the cache; if missing, check the source.

Tradeoff: faster reads, but extra storage and possibly stale data.

rigorous.name: Careful reasoning
rigorous.description: Define terms, trace the reasoning and examine its limits.
rigorous.example:
Assume data is stored somewhere relatively slow and the same data is read repeatedly. A cache keeps copies to reduce access to that slower store.

Finding the requested data in the cache is a hit. Otherwise, the request must reach the original source and may populate the cache.

The benefit depends on hit rate and maintenance cost. Rarely reused or frequently changing data may gain little. Consistency between the copy and its source also needs a policy.
